description: Preceded by years of strong credit growth and a housing-price boom: the ratio of bank loans to nominal GDP rose from about 35 percent to over 70 percent between about 1880 and 1891, then plunged to about 40 percent by 1900. The 1880s credit expansion was financed by large capital inflows, especially from the UK; when Barings faced liquidity problems over its Argentine investments (Baring Crisis of 1890), attention turned to all overseas securities and a sudden stop of capital inflows to Australia followed, producing financial distress. In the first five months of 1893, 13 trading banks were forced to close their doors and had to write off 40 percent of their initial capital in the same year. No government rescue is described.
sources: Fisher & Kent (1999, p. 7); Aliber & Kindleberger (2015, p. 196); Fisher & Kent (1999)

description: Banking reform and credit-market liberalization from the late 1970s increased competition and allowed banks to invest in higher-risk assets; through the 1980s banks rapidly increased exposures and asset prices rose. When the economy slowed in 1989 the banking system faced mounting non-performing loans. Two large banks had to be rescued by the government (Section 5.1 names them as the State Bank of South Australia (SBSA) and the State Bank of Victoria (STV), which effectively failed and relied on extraordinary government support). The ratio of current losses to the average value of banks' lending rose from nearly zero to about 3 percent during 1989, and between 1990 and 1993 about 12 percent of all business loans in the Australian banking system were non-performing on average. Not coded by Laeven & Valencia (2018); see Section 5.1.
sources: Caprio & Klingebiel (2003, p. 15); Rodgers (2015, p. 10); Rodgers (2015, p. 13)

description: Banking panic as described by Buyst & Maes (2007): frightened by the threat of war between France and Prussia, the Belgian Finance Minister and the governor of the National Bank of Belgium (NBB) ordered the immediate evacuation of the metal reserves out of the capital; the removal caused such commotion that it sparked panic among the population, who besieged the NBB's head office demanding conversion of notes into coins. The NBB responded by closing its counters except one, and the volume of discount transactions was reduced drastically. Not coded by Baron et al. (2021); Section 5.3 justifies the coding by the extensive bank panic that made it necessary to close the central bank and the bank counters.
sources: Buyst & Maes (2007); Buyst & Maes (2007, pp. 131-132)

description: The collapse of a major railway corporation created distrust in the financial system which, according to Buyst & Maes (2007), developed into a financial crisis in which several banks went bankrupt. Grossman (2010) summarises: a substantial boom in the early 1870s, fuelled partly by the Franco-Prussian War, led to the establishment of a number of new banks; several failed when the international crisis hit the Brussels Stock Exchange; a few smaller banks went into receivership and three larger banks (Banque de Belgique, Banque de Bruxelles, Banque Centrale Anversoise) had to be reorganized. Newly added crisis year in this version of the chronology (Section 3.1), following Baron et al. (2021); not in crisisJST_old. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis.
sources: Buyst & Maes (2007, pp. 135-136); Grossman (2010, p. 299)

description: In the late 1870s many Belgian banks introduced interest-bearing short-term current accounts to encourage use of the payment system, which as a side effect increased the danger of illiquidity from cash withdrawals. Buyst & Maes (2007) argue this danger materialized in 1885, with many banks becoming illiquid. The Belgian central bank refused to act as lender of last resort. Financially weak banks, including Banque de Belgique, and other institutions such as Banque des Travaux Publics failed; by estimate more than 20 percent of total paid-up capital in the Belgian banking sector had to be written off. Not identified by Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009); Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1883.
sources: Buyst & Maes (2009, p. 99); Buyst & Maes (2007, pp. 136-139)

description: Fears of a currency devaluation in 1925 led to panic deposit withdrawals and worsened the financing conditions of firms and banks. The continuing devaluation of the Belgian franc during 1926 forced the Belgian government to borrow in US dollars to cover Belgian notes and banks, and throughout 1926 the banking system consolidated through mergers. Not coded by Baron et al. (2021); Section 5.3 justifies the coding by the government borrowing in USD to guarantee the liabilities of Belgian banks and the increased merger activity. No source citation is given in the narrative.

As a small open economy Belgium was hit hard by the worldwide decline in foreign demand; banks were exposed to the export industry both as creditors and as major shareholders of export-oriented firms. Defaults and bankruptcies of a significant number of export firms forced several medium-sized banks to suspend payments, and rumors about the failure of Banque de Bruxelles, one of the country's largest banks, led to further declines in confidence and withdrawals from all banks. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1929.
sources: Buyst & Maes (2009, pp. 100-102); Bernanke & James (1991, p. 91)

description: In March 1934 the large Banque Belge du Travail went bankrupt, causing a loss of public confidence and a first wave of deposit withdrawals. The government responded with structural reform requiring universal banks to split into deposit-taking institutions and holding companies. Despite this, the deteriorating situation of Algemeene Bankvereeniging threatened to bring down Middenkredietkas, the bank of Belgium's Catholic Farmers league, which would have wiped out the savings of thousands of peasants. At the end of 1934 rumors of an impending bankruptcy of Algemeene Bankvereeniging and Middenkredietkas triggered further mass withdrawals and a general crisis of confidence with large-scale capital flight. A government of national unity formed in 1935 under NBB vice-governor Paul van Zeeland at King Leopold III's request devalued the franc and established a banking supervision authority. Not coded by Baron et al. (2021); Section 5.3 cites the bank runs provoked by the Banque du Travail failure and the government's active intervention to stabilize the banks.
sources: Buyst & Maes (2009, pp. 102-103); Mommen (1994, p. 23); Buyst & Maes (2009, p. 103); Giddey (2014)

description: Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) note that the economy was slowly recovering until the prospect of war hampered investment decisions, so that foreign exchange and gold reserves diminished dramatically. Baron et al. (2019) identify a decline of bank equity prices of around 50 percent on the Belgian stock market. Two large banks failed: Crédit Anversois in 1939 and Caisse Générale Reports et Dépôts in 1940, the latter dragged down partly by the bankruptcy of the Dutch banking house Mendelssohn & Cie. Figures from the Commission Bancaire (Belgium's banking supervisor) show a marked reduction in the total number of banks operating in Belgium between 1939 and 1940. Marked as not identified (X) by Baron et al. (2021) in the Section 4 comparison table, but not discussed in Section 5.3.
sources: Reinhart & Rogoff (2009, p. 325); Baron et al. (2019); Giddey (2017); Giddey (2017, p. 9)

description: Part of the international financial crisis that started in the United States. Two of Belgium's largest banks, Fortis and Dexia, faced declining capital and increasing write-offs, lost access to the overnight interbank market and had to turn to the Eurosystem's Marginal Lending Facility. In late 2008 the Belgian operations of Fortis were nationalized with a EUR 4.7 billion capital injection by the Belgian government; Dexia was supported with a EUR 6.4 billion capital injection and EUR 150 billion in public guarantees under an agreement between Belgium, France and Luxembourg. Belgium's measures and commitments to support financial institutions amounted to 47 percent of GDP by 2010. Baron et al. (2021) additionally flag 2011, which JST treats as linked to the 2008 crisis (Section 5.4).
sources: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2010); Wiggins et al. (2014a); Wiggins et al. (2014b); Stolz & Wedow (2010, pp. 19-21)

description: The financial panic of 1907 in Canada may have been part of the international panic that started in the United States (Rich (1989) gives a broad discussion). Increasing volatility in money demand raised money market rates and made bank financing more difficult; loss of confidence aggravated the situation. In 1907 and 1908 three Canadian banks failed. When the Sovereign Bank of Canada failed in 1908, the Bank of Montreal stepped in to coordinate a response by other banks. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) date the episode to 1908; Bordo et al. (2001) do not identify a crisis. Canada's only coded episode; the Baron et al. (2021) years 1873, 1920 and 1983 are explicitly rejected (Section 5.4).
sources: Rich (1989); Calomiris & Haber (2014, pp. 305-307)

description: Quoted from Grossman (2010): Switzerland was highly dependent on the French monetary and financial systems; the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War and France's unilateral extension of maturity on commercial bills cut Switzerland off from its main sources of coins and credit. No bank failures or policy response are described in the narrative.
sources: Grossman (2010, p. 310)

description: Vogler (2001) describes a wave of major bank collapses, particularly 1910-1913 and again during the First World War: between 1910 and 1913, 45 local and regional banks collectively incurred losses of CHF 112 million, equivalent to the size of the Confederation's budget in 1912, and 28 banks merged with either a cantonal or a major bank (85 in the decade from 1906). The contemporary economist Ernst Wetter attributed the collapses to 'personal' reasons (failure of executives) and 'factual' reasons such as inadequate regulatory oversight and bad business policies; banks had engaged in very speculative lending and financial planning with an already extremely inadequate liquidity situation, and Wetter (1918) also cites insufficient risk distribution within the banking system and a lack of transparency in published banking data. Not coded by Baron et al. (2021) or Bordo et al. (2001); Section 5.3 justifies the coding by the CHF 112 million losses of 45 banks and the 28 mergers.
sources: Vogler (2001); Wetter (1918)

description: Zurlinden (2003) describes Switzerland as a victim of the gold standard: the economic collapse in the US, Germany, France and the UK cut external demand for Swiss industrial goods, exports fell by more than 50 percent between 1929 and 1932, and the devaluations by the UK, Germany and others from 1931 eroded Swiss competitiveness. During 1931 and the following years bank bankruptcies and the losses of the whole banking system increased; bank stock prices fell 50 percent in 1931 alone. The Swiss 'Big Banks' were especially affected: the Swiss Bank and the Banque d'Escompte Suisse were forced to turn to the government for assistance. In July 1931 the Union Financière de Genève went into financial distress and was rescued by a takeover by the Comptoir d'Escompte de Genève.
sources: Zurlinden (2003); Zurlinden (2003, pp. 109-112); Bernanke & James (1991, p. 92)

description: Real estate prices doubled over the 1980s; in 1991 they started to fall rapidly, producing estimated losses of about CHF 42 billion (roughly 8.5 percent of total loan volume, or more than 10 percent of Swiss GDP). The big banks alone wrote off CHF 30 billion, nearly 13 percent of their loan volume. Banks faced problems on both sides of the balance sheet (refinancing existing loans and huge write-offs). About half of the 200 regional banks disappeared; almost all troubled banks merged with stronger banks and only a single bank had to be liquidated. Not coded by Laeven & Valencia (2018), Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009); Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1990. Section 5.1 justifies the coding by the loan losses, the 200 banks that did not survive and lost their independence, and the forced mergers.
sources: Sources: Ziegler (2004)

description: Switzerland was hit by the international financial crisis through two channels: the large Swiss banks' high exposures to the US real estate market, and the worldwide downturn that reduced foreign demand and exports. The global banks UBS and Credit Suisse were majorly affected and had to publicly announce losses and write-offs. The Swiss government, the Swiss National Bank and the Swiss Federal Banking Commission announced a package of measures to stabilize the financial system, including the possibility for UBS to transfer a portfolio of illiquid assets to a fund entity managed by the SNB and a CHF 6 billion recapitalisation of UBS directed by the government.
sources: Swiss National Bank (2009, pp. 21-22)

description: The year of the 'Gründerkrach'. Technological progress in the late 1860s led to an economic boom in Prussia, a surge in construction and company formation. After the founding of the Kaiserreich and victory over France, reparation payments were used to increase the money supply and reduce government debt, lowering outstanding government bonds; stronger economic integration and the liberalization of stock corporation law reinforced the expansion and increasingly channelled private capital into shares, which ultimately led to the stock market crash and banking crisis of 1873. Many banks engaged in financing the newly founded companies were affected and had to close their doors. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1874.
sources: Brunnermeier & Schnabel (2016, pp. 42-45); Plumpe (2012, pp. 62-67)

description: A consequence of the Baring Crisis of 1890: the growing role of the international gold standard led to strong capital outflows from European countries, including Germany, to the rest of the world, and when Barings went into distress over Argentine defaults many German banks were affected. The turmoil led to the bankruptcy of the bank Hirschfeld & Wolff and revealed fraudulent behaviour and exposure to risky stocks; the bankruptcy of a well-respected bank as a result of fraud caused a bank run and brought down other major banks associated with questionable stock market deals. Neither Bordo et al. (2001) nor Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) do.
sources: Grossman (2010, p. 307); Tilly (2013)

description: After an expansion from 1894, many German banks in the late 1890s invested in Russian companies and strong capital inflows drove up prices in Russia; when prices fell, Russian companies incurred heavy losses that hit invested banks in Germany and Belgium. The bankruptcy of Leipziger Bank laid bare large-scale fraud at a bank once considered rock-solid: managers had hidden its exposure to 'Trebergesellschaft', a large joint-stock company that had reported fake profits for several years. In the following turmoil another large bank, the Dresdner Creditanstalt, also went bankrupt. The crisis marked the end of the post-1894 expansion. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Bordo et al. (2001) and Baron et al. (2021) do.

Following Schnabel (2004): from 1925 huge foreign capital inflows financed a significant credit expansion, leaving the banking system vulnerable because banks funded risky projects with short-term foreign debt. When US interest rates rose, foreign capital was withdrawn and tensions in private banking grew. In May 1931 the recession, political uncertainty over reparations and the bankruptcy of the Österreichische Creditanstalt triggered a banking panic in Germany: from June 1930 to July 1931 domestic deposits at the most relevant German banks fell 20 percent and foreign deposits on average 30 percent. Until 1932 the government assisted private banks with 910.3 million Reichsmark and public banks with 62.5 million Reichsmark. One of the big banks, 54 provincial banks and about 400 private banks failed; despite government assistance, bank capital declined by over 32 percent. Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1930.
sources: Schnabel (2004); Schnabel (2004, p. 856); Fischer (2013, p. 262)

description: Part of the international crisis that erupted in the US after the sharp fall in real estate prices. Shin (2012) argues German banks were strongly affected because of their pivotal role in US intermediation: by providing credit to the US shadow banking system they bought private-label mortgage-backed securities and other structured products, so active participation in securitization left substantial toxic assets on their balance sheets. The public-law Landesbanken were the main participants and were primarily hit, making a broader government bail-out necessary; Commerzbank, one of Germany's largest private banks, needed government recapitalization. At the peak 3.7 percent of all loans in the German banking system were non-performing. Germany's measures and commitments to support financial institutions amounted to 25 percent of GDP (based on 2008).
sources: Shin (2012); Sources: Stolz & Wedow (2010), Shin (2012), Rudolph (2013), Hellwig (2017), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: Part of the broader financial turmoil of the 1870s that started with the German Gründerkrach. Several savings banks and a few commercial banks experienced a crisis during the recession, and the Danish Nationalbank had to provide extraordinary loans to banks. Not covered by Bordo et al. (2001); identified by Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) and Baron et al. (2021).
sources: Sources: Grossman (2010, p. 301), Abildgren et al. (2011)

description: During a wave of bankruptcies the liquidity of the Danish banking system came under pressure and the National Bank of Denmark intervened as lender of last resort.
sources: Abildgren et al. (2011, p. 6)

description: Part of the international panic that started in the US in 1907 and spread to several European countries. Danish banks had built up portfolios during the 1901-1906 boom that were hit by the panic. The Freeholders' Bank (Grundejerbank) suspended, followed by a run on several institutions and a serious decline in the value of bank shares (the Retailers' Bank, Detailhandlerbank, lost twenty points). The government, Danmarks Nationalbank and a number of large private banks established a Banking Committee to provide guarantees for depositors and other creditors of crisis-stricken banks, and Denmark's largest savings bank was reconstructed with government help. Bordo et al. (2001), Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) and Baron et al. (2021) all date the episode to 1907.
sources: Hansen (1991, p. 39); Conant (1915, pp. 300-301); Abildgren et al. (2011, p. 6)

description: Wartime government interventions increased liquidity that banks used to expand their stock investments; despite low growth, share prices accelerated and tripled until 1918. When the international deflationary crisis hit at the beginning of the 1920s share prices fell significantly and a systemic banking crisis followed in which a total of 23 Danish banks had to be liquidated, restructured with government assistance, or acquired by larger banks. Landmandsbank, the largest bank in Denmark, recorded heavy losses and was recapitalized by the government. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1919.
sources: Hansen (2012, pp. 678-679); Hansen (2012, p. 679); Abildgren et al. (2011, p. 6)

description: After deregulation in the late 1970s and early 1980s, higher growth and capital inflows went hand in hand with rising asset prices. In 1987 Denmark experienced financial instability in which a number of banks encountered difficulties, including the ninth largest bank, Varde Bank; the government and Danmarks Nationalbank were involved in finding solutions for five distressed banks. Not coded by Laeven & Valencia (2018) or Baron et al. (2021). Section 5.1 adds that 142 banks were involved in 75 mergers and acquisitions, cumulated losses over 1990-1992 were 9 percent of loans, and large losses of capital resulted in forced mergers; Section 5.3 states 1987 was coded because it is considered the starting point of the Nordic Banking Crisis in Denmark; Section 5.4 rejects the Baron et al. (2021) year 1992 because the crisis stretched over several years from 1987.
sources: Abildgren et al. (2011, p. 6); Sources: Vastrup (2009), Abildgren et al. (2011)

description: Part of the 2008/2009 international crisis, but with causes both abroad and in domestic developments: the Committee of the Causes of the Financial Crisis (2013) concludes that rising real estate prices and increased risk-taking by Danish banks in domestic markets were important, and participation in securitization brought substantial toxic assets onto Danish balance sheets. Denmark faced a banking panic in which many banks had to be shut down, restructured or acquired, including four of the 15 largest banks; at the peak 9.4 percent of all loans were non-performing. The government and the central bank intervened heavily; Denmark's support measures and commitments amounted to 23 percent of GDP (based on 2008). Baron et al. (2021) additionally flag 2011, which JST rejects as showing no banking panic or systemic risks (Section 5.4).
sources: Committee of the Causes of the Financial Crisis (2013); Laeven & Valencia (2018); Abildgren et al. (2011, p. 6); Sources: Stolz & Wedow (2010, p. 20), Abildgren et al. (2011), Committee of the Causes of the Financial Crisis (2013), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: Associated with the 'gold fever' that produced a strong equity price boom and higher capital inflows in the early 1880s. Economic turmoil in Spain and the French crisis after the stock market crash of 1882 led to a sudden reversal of capital flows, and the reserve losses of the Spanish central bank motivated its decision to abandon the gold standard temporarily. Between 1882 and 1884 twenty banks disappeared, most of them from Barcelona. Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010) argue that the collapse of many systemic banks in Spain's big cities triggered a decline in loan supply and was a leading factor in the stagnation of the following years. Not identified by Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009); Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1882.
sources: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010, p. 13); Betrán & Pons (2013, pp. 18-19); Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010)

description: A consequence of the Baring Crisis of 1890: the growing role of the international gold standard induced strong capital outflows from Europe, and when Barings went into distress over Argentine defaults a financial crisis hit many Spanish securities on domestic and foreign markets. Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010) describe the sharp decline of stock prices as the trigger for rising liquidity and cash ratios and declining loan supply and investment by banks. Two banks were liquidated and the damage to the financial structure continued to burden banks for many years after the event. Not identified by Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009); identified by Baron et al. (2021).
sources: Betrán & Pons (2013, pp. 19-20); Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010)

description: Characterized by financial distress at the Banco Hispano Americano, a large institution, with direct consequences for other banks and a halt to its involvement in Latin America. It was the first time the Bank of Spain intervened as lender of last resort to prevent the situation from worsening. Betrán et al. (2012) identify a 44 percent decline in real bank stock prices between 1910 and 1916. Not identified by Bordo et al. (2001), Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) or Baron et al. (2021); Section 5.3 justifies the coding by the first-ever lender-of-last-resort intervention of the Spanish central bank and the significant decline in real bank stock prices.
sources: Betrán et al. (2012, p. 422); Sources: Betrán et al. (2012), Betrán et al. (2014, pp. 42-44)

description: During the First World War the Spanish banking system expanded its links with many industries, extending credit for capital-intensive investment and increasingly taking property as collateral; after the war much production capacity remained idle, with negative consequences for the intermediaries that had granted the loans. In 1920 turmoil began when the Bank of Barcelona failed; a banking panic followed, necessitating cautious intervention by the Bank of Spain to assist the banking system with liquidity. Stock returns from 1919 to 1920 amounted to -13 percent.
sources: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010, pp. 21-22); Betrán et al. (2012, p. 422)

description: The banking system had not recovered from the 1920 crisis and still carried many bad loans and devalued stocks; policymakers were unable to reform the institutional framework. When a recession hit in 1924 a bank run destabilized the system further, and the ratio of bank deposits to currency began to decline in 1924. The Banco de la Union Mineira and the Banco Vasca, together with eight other banks, went bankrupt.
sources: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010); Betrán et al. (2012, p. 423)

description: Followed strong domestic political upheavals and was also a consequence of the global crisis that started in the US; rising political uncertainty, economic crises in neighbouring countries and financial distress started a banking panic in Spain. Unlike many other countries, Spain contained the damage through cooperation between the central bank, acting as lender of last resort, and the government. During the panic three banks failed and stock prices declined significantly; four affected Spanish banks failed over the following years.
sources: Betrán et al. (2012, p. 423); Sources: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010, pp. 25-26), Betrán et al. (2012)

description: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010) attribute the crisis to a combination of exogenous and endogenous shocks: the oil price shocks of the 1970s, deteriorating competitiveness of Spanish industry and high risk-taking by banks after the credit-market liberalizations of the 1960s. About 52 banks representing 20 percent of deposits struggled with solvency problems and had to be saved through interventions of the government and the central bank; many were restructured and sold to other banks or merged to prevent massive losses. At the peak 5.8 percent of all loans were non-performing, and an intense period of financial restructuring followed the resolution of the crisis. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1975.
sources: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010); Laeven & Valencia (2018); Sources: Martín-Aceña & Pons (2010, pp. 37-41), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: Parallel to the US crisis. Euro adoption produced a convergence of interest rates followed by years of higher growth, rising real estate prices and large current account deficits vis-a-vis other Eurozone countries; when real estate prices started to decline the banking system faced high write-offs. Betrán et al. (2012) identify a banking crisis and emphasize that the number of savings banks dropped from 45 to 2. At the peak 5.8 percent of all loans were non-performing. The government intervened with a vast bank recapitalization program and the ECB acted as lender of last resort; Spain's support measures and commitments amounted to 23 percent of GDP (based on 2008). Baron et al. (2021) additionally flag 2010, which JST treats as linked to the 2008 crisis (Section 5.4).
sources: Betrán et al. (2012); Laeven & Valencia (2018); Sources: Stolz & Wedow (2010, p. 20), Betrán et al. (2012), Martín-Aceña (2014), Aliber & Kindleberger (2015), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: After the Franco-Prussian War, rising European demand for Finnish forest products drove up asset prices, increased the exposure of Finnish banks and took on increasingly speculative traits; the subsequent fall in forest-product prices caused high write-offs at the affected banks. The bankruptcy of a Russian subsidiary of the largest Finnish bank, Pohjoismaiden Osakepankki, was the catalyst for a decline in profits that spread through the banking system. Bank profitability in proportion to total assets was -1.1 percent in 1877. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) do.
sources: Sources: Herrala (1999)

description: Following Herrala (1999): the Finnish Agriculture and Industry Bank, founded in 1897, ran a very risk-based strategy of speculative investment, aggressive interest-rate competition, active marketing for deposits and even fraudulent practices, and depended on central bank financing. When a recession started at the turn of the century the bank fell into financial distress and ultimately failed, causing losses to its depositors. Financial contagion was contained through public intervention. Bank profitability in proportion to total assets was -0.4 percent in 1900. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Bordo et al. (2001) and Baron et al. (2021) do.
sources: Herrala (1999)

description: Strong inflation in 1914-1917 brought a sharp decline in real activity, yet share prices rose and many new, small, specialized banks were established on the credit markets. At the beginning of the 1920s a sharp depreciation of the markka hit many of those newly founded, highly exposed banks and started a banking crisis, which also ended the recovery under way since the end of the civil war. Bank mergers were used to stabilize the banking system, but there were still high losses in the financial system and write-offs for creditors and depositors. Bank profitability in proportion to total assets was -0.2 percent in 1921.
sources: Sources: Herrala (1999)

description: Economic recovery in 1925-1928 was accompanied by increased speculative activity by financial institutions; a poor harvest in 1928 ended the expansion and started a recession. The real problems in the financial system surfaced at the beginning of the 1930 world economic crisis, which sharply hit Finnish exports and deepened the recession. Herrala (1999) describes the events of 1931 as a capital market failure after domestic and foreign shocks, leading to an asset-price decline that affected several banks, with a significant decline in the number of bank branches. Bank profitability in proportion to total assets was -0.5 percent in 1931.
sources: Herrala (1999); Sources: Herrala (1999)

description: Financial liberalization and a fixed exchange rate at the beginning of the 1980s catalysed strong international capital inflows; Jonung et al. (2009a) emphasize that households took on high debt to finance a sharp increase in consumption and investment. Between 1989 and 1991 Finland faced rising interest rates and the collapse of the Soviet Union, one of its leading trading partners. Significant write-offs followed and non-performing loans rose to 13 percent of all loans. Three banks were taken over by the state (Skopbank, the Savings Bank of Finland and the STS-bank) and the remainder of the banking system became dependent on government support. Government recapitalization costs amounted to 8.63 percent of GDP. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1990.
sources: Jonung et al. (2009a); Englund & Vihriälä (2009, pp. 91-93)

description: During the 1870s private investors and banks increased their exposure to the Paris Bourse and financed share purchases with loans in expectation of rising stock prices. When interest rates in Europe started to rise, stock prices fell rapidly, causing high write-offs especially on the forward markets. The decline hit primarily the Union Générale, which experienced intense financial distress, and the resulting losses created a banking panic that had to be contained through loan support from the Bank of France and several private banks. Seven stockbrokers at the Paris Bourse and nine at the Lyon Bourse, together with the entire Lyon Bourse, failed; runs on and subsequent failures of the Banque de Lyon and Union Générale burdened the financial system.
sources: Sources: White (2007), Brunnermeier & Schnabel (2016)

description: Following Hautcoeur et al. (2014): the copper industrialist Secrètan, aiming at a global copper monopoly, had his company, the Société Industrielle et Commerciale des Métaux (SdM), acquire a large number of copper mine shares and use futures contracts to raise the copper price and the company's value, financed by extensive loans from commercial and investment banks and by (off-balance-sheet) guarantees of the risks. When copper prices plummeted, participating banks suffered massive losses and the Comptoir d'Escompte (CdE), classified by observers as systemically relevant, was on the verge of insolvency. The Bank of France reacted by creating a 'lifeboat' to support the CdE and provided a loan of 100 million francs to prevent a potential banking panic.
sources: Hautcoeur et al. (2014)

description: Part of the world economic crisis that started in the US in 1929. From 1930 to 1936 France experienced stagnating industrial production, falling prices, rising unemployment and deteriorating competitiveness because it remained on the gold standard until 1936 while many countries withdrew. Grossman (2010) lists failures of local banks (Banque Adam, Oustric Group, Banque Renauld, Charpenay, Veuve Guérin), a regional bank (Banque d'Alsace-Lorraine) and the national Banque Nationale de Crédit (1930-1931); a major investment bank, Banque de l'Union Parisienne (1932), was rescued by the Bank of France working with Paris banks. Further bank failures, bank runs and increased losses within the banking system occurred in the following years.
sources: Sauvy (1969); Grossman (2010, p. 314); Bernanke & James (1991, pp. 51-53)

description: Part of the international crisis that started in the US; French banks were exposed to the US real estate market. When US and European real estate prices declined, write-offs and losses followed, with BNP Paribas in the focus of public attention after announcing its losses. France introduced guarantees of about EUR 360 billion for French credit institutions and provided a EUR 55 billion guarantee for Dexia as part of an agreement with Belgium and Luxembourg. At the peak 4.5 percent of all loans in the French banking system were non-performing. Support measures and commitments amounted to 18 percent of GDP (based on 2008).
sources: Shin (2012); Sources: Stolz & Wedow (2010, pp. 19-20), Shin (2012), Cecchetti & Schoenholtz (2017), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: The Baring Crisis. During the 1880s huge capital flows from Europe, especially Britain, went to Argentina, where investment took on increasingly speculative traits; Baring Brothers and Co., which underwrote most of Argentina's debt issues, was at the centre. In 1890 Argentina's high public debt and economic and banking problems reduced foreign trust in Argentinian securities and led to default on those loans, creating a global financial panic with many banks trying to sell distressed securities, whose fire sales further destabilized the affected banks. Barings had to accept high losses, threatening a collapse of the British financial system. To prevent contagion the Bank of England, the Bank of France and the Bank of Russia, together with several British private investors, created a rescue fund to save the institution. Further effects on the British economy were manageable.
sources: Sources: Paolera & Taylor (2001), Mitchener & Weidenmier (2008)

description: The 'Secondary Banking Crisis'. Many new financial intermediaries arose in the 1960s which, unlike the 'primary' banks, funded themselves on the wholesale market and pushed into property and consumer loans. In 1970 the government adopted a growth strategy of moderate bank deregulation, more competition between intermediaries and expansive monetary policy, accompanied by a credit boom and booms in several property markets and share prices. The secondary banks financed long-term loans with very short-term liquidity; when inflation rose in 1973 asset prices fell and they could not refinance existing loans. The Bank of England and the government intervened vastly to protect the primary banks from contagion and the huge write-offs of the secondary banks: a 'lifeboat' of GBP 1.2 billion provided emergency loans to 24 distressed secondary banks; of a further 26 distressed secondary banks that received no support, eight collapsed and most of the others were merged. Not coded by Laeven & Valencia (2018) (Section 5.1); Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1973.
sources: Sources: Reid (1982)

description: The 1980s liberalization of the British banking system and capital markets was followed by a sharp increase in mortgage lending and household debt with lower lending standards (Balluck et al., 2016). The UK joined the European exchange-rate system in 1990, obliging a fixed rate to the Deutschmark; when German reunification raised interest rates, the UK faced speculative attacks on the exchange rate and losses in the banking system from defaulting loans. Many banks had funding problems and the danger of contagion led to an intervention by the Bank of England. The crisis led to the failure of 25 small banks and write-offs of about 2 percent of total loans. Not coded by Laeven & Valencia (2018) or Bordo et al. (2001); Section 5.1 notes the Bank of England's emergency loans to British banks and that 25 banks failed until 1994 due to loan defaults and loss of capital.
sources: Balluck et al. (2016)

description: Part of the international crisis but with similarities to the US: UK banks concentrated essential parts of their business model on real estate, used securitization and became increasingly dependent on short-term wholesale funding. UK real estate prices rose significantly from 1997 to 2007 and started declining in mid-2007, inducing losses in the banking system; consequences included financial contagion and a run on Northern Rock. The government and the Bank of England reacted with sizeable intervention: nationalization of Northern Rock and guarantees on short- to medium-term bank debt. The UK's support measures and commitments amounted to 25 percent of GDP (based on 2008). NOTE: the narrative heading dates this episode GBR-2007, but the Section 4 comparison table lists the UK crisis year as 2008 (with Baron et al. (2021) at 2007); the narrative heading year is used here and the discrepancy should be checked against the dataset.
sources: Sources: Barrell & Davis (2008), Shin (2009), Stolz & Wedow (2010)

description: Preceded by a massive credit expansion, with non-financial lending more than tripling from its 1997 level. Banks financed a property bubble that came to a halt in 2007 when financial sector stocks began to trend downwards. In 2008 Irish banks, which had borrowed heavily on international markets, were hit by short-term interest rates on international interbank markets; the liquidity squeeze aggravated asset-side problems and the stock prices of the three largest banks (Anglo Irish, Bank of Ireland, AIB) fell steeply, AIB from a peak of EUR 23.95 in February 2007 to EUR 0.28 by March 2009. The government nationalized Anglo Irish Bank in January 2009 and injected equity into AIB and Bank of Ireland, in addition to ECB loans amounting to EUR 17 billion and EUR 34 billion respectively by August 2009. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 2007; Section 5.4 explains that Irish bank stocks fell in 2007 on rising mortgage defaults but the banks collapsed in 2008 as part of the global liquidity crisis. Not covered by Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009).
sources: Kelly (2009); Centonze (2014); Honohan (2019, p. 106); Centonze (2014); Kelly (2009)

description: Increased liquidity in the late 1860s expanded Italian banks' lending, including financing of railroads and other businesses; the German Gründerkrach and the end of the US railroad boom spread to Europe and affected Italian banks. Bartoletto et al. (2018) argue the banks of issue were especially hit, while Gigliobianco & Giordano (2010) emphasize losses of private bankers and of savings and cooperative banks. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) do.
sources: Bartoletto et al. (2018, pp. 13-14); Gigliobianco & Giordano (2010, p. 13); Sources: Grossman (2010, p. 307), Gigliobianco & Giordano (2010), Bartoletto et al. (2018)

description: In a regulatory 'vacuum' and with an expansionary monetary stance, Italian banks expanded real estate credit as exposures and property prices rose; in 1887 real estate prices began to decline and the involved banks incurred losses, exacerbated by a trade war with France. Capital inflow dried up and reversed by the late 1880s, and banks continued to suffer from the sharp decline in real estate prices and rising non-performing loans. The Banca Tiberiana and the Banco di Sconto e Sete failed. Non-performing loans of commercial banks are estimated to have risen from 1 to 8 percent by 1891. Bordo et al. (2001) do not identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1889.
sources: Bartoletto et al. (2018, p. 8); Fratianni & Spinelli (1997, p. 88)

description: Growing demand for industrial and residential real estate financing in the 1880s, with wild speculation in land development and construction relying mostly on short-term bank credit, generated excess supply, a drop in prices and failures of real estate companies and banks (Fratianni & Spinelli, 1997). The authorities pressured the banks, despite their own losses, to support failing commercial banks. The unresolved problems of the 1887 crisis ultimately led to the failure of Banca Romana, Credito Mobiliare and Banca Generale. As a result the banking system was reorganized and four troubled banks were merged to create the Bank of Italy. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1891.
sources: Fratianni & Spinelli (1997, p. 87); Toniolo (1995, p. 297); Sources: Toniolo (1995), Fratianni & Spinelli (1997), Grossman (2010)

description: Rising interest rates had already slowed Italian stock markets by the end of 1906; in 1907 the mis-speculation of several relevant US financiers triggered a financial panic that affected several European countries. Italian banks reduced their stock market exposure, equity prices declined, and despite Bank of Italy interventions the declines generated fear of a credit crunch while rising deposit withdrawals weakened the liquidity position of the banking system. One of the main universal banks, the Società Bancaria Italiana, was on the verge of bankruptcy. The crisis was contained through the first huge-scale intervention by the Bank of Italy.
sources: Sources: Gigliobianco et al. (2009), Bartoletto et al. (2018, pp. 16-17)

description: Centred on the Banca Italiana di Sconto, which had granted a substantial part of its loans to war-related industry; private or public support came too late and liquidation was inevitable. At the same time the Banco di Roma suffered enormous losses of deposits and posed a risk to the economy as a whole, but was rescued with public funds. From 1919 to 1922 the ratio of bank assets to GDP fell from 0.307 to 0.273 and the ratio of bank assets to total assets from 0.624 to 0.467. No source citation is given in the narrative.

Italy was hit by the international crisis that started in the US at the end of 1929; its membership in the gold standard is described as a main reason for the substantial capital outflows and the onset of deflation. In December 1930 a deposit withdrawal hit the three largest Italian banks. In 1931 the government started a vast and secret intervention to stabilize the most important Italian banks; Toniolo (1995) emphasizes it was carried out with such discretion that the Italian public did not realize the depth of the crisis.
sources: Toniolo (1995, pp. 307-308); Sources: Bernanke & James (1991), Toniolo (1995), Gigliobianco & Giordano (2010)

description: After a brief recovery in credit aggregates following the 1930/1931 crisis, loans contracted sharply in 1935. Major bankruptcies of Italian banks were prevented by interventions of the Bank of Italy and the Italian government. Bernanke & James (1991) emphasize the sharp decline in deposits and point to the invasion of Abyssinia as a reason for the problems. Not coded by Baron et al. (2021); Section 5.3 justifies the coding by the crucial role of the government and the Bank of Italy in overcoming the crisis and preventing major banks from failing.
sources: Bernanke & James (1991, p. 53); Sources: Bernanke & James (1991), Bartoletto et al. (2018, pp. 10-11)

description: Bartoletto et al. (2018) argue the Italian banking system already had several structural problems when external shocks (the crisis of the European Monetary System and political upheavals) destabilized it further. A substantial rise in interest rates after German reunification provoked speculative attacks on the lira that led to Italy's withdrawal from the EMS. Non-performing loans rose to 5.7 percent of aggregate loans in 1993 and 7.9 percent in 1995 in the centre-north banking system, and to 10.2 percent (1993) and 25.4 percent (1995) in the southern banking system. During 1990-94, 58 banks accounting for 11 percent of lending were merged with other institutions. Not coded by Laeven & Valencia (2018); Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1992. Section 5.1 cites the 58 mergers and the rise of southern NPLs from 10.2 to 25.4 percent (which it dates 1993 to 1996).
sources: Bartoletto et al. (2018); Caprio & Klingebiel (2003, p. 15); Sources: Fratianni & Spinelli (1997), Caprio & Klingebiel (2003), Bartoletto et al. (2018, pp. 11-12)

description: Italy was not directly affected by the international crisis because its banks had low exposures to complex financial products, but they faced falling international confidence and an abrupt stop of international capital flows. The government put in place a recapitalization program to stabilize sound banks, used by Banco Popolare Società Cooperativa for a total of EUR 1.45 billion. In September 2008 about 18 percent of all loans in the Italian banking system were non-performing. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Laeven & Valencia (2018) and Baron et al. (2021) do. Baron et al. (2021) additionally flag 2011, which JST rejects: despite an increase in financial stress there was no systemic crisis (Section 5.4).
sources: European Commission (2009); Sources: European Commission (2009), Bank of Italy (2010, pp. 141-145), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: In 1871 the government of Japan declared it would adopt the gold standard and introduced the yen as the new unit of account, issuing gold coins for general use and silver coins for international trade. Grossman (2010) argues this reform led to the failure of nine out of ten exchange companies, the precursors of banks that had been established to provide banking services. Not identified by Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) or Baron et al. (2021); Section 5.3 justifies the coding by the failure of nine out of ten exchange companies.
sources: Grossman (2010, p. 308)

description: In the mid-1880s the Tokyo Stock Exchange became an essential marketplace for share trading, and many corporations, especially listed ones, had borrowed large amounts of capital from banks. When a bad harvest in autumn 1889 brought large pecuniary demands, a banking panic occurred. The newly founded Bank of Japan had to intervene as lender of last resort. Not identified by Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009); identified by Baron et al. (2021).
sources: Tamaki (1995, p. 66)

description: In the mid-1890s many banks concentrated on financing the country's long-term industrial development and the number of banks rose sharply from about 500 to about 2500, with the 1893 legal framework for commercial banking as a significant change. Okazaki & Yokoyama (2002) describe the 1901 crisis as a financial (banking) panic that also marks the peak of the boom of newly founded banks; the panic led many banks to fail and reversed the trend in the number of operating banks. Newly added crisis year in this version (Section 3.1), following Baron et al. (2021): described as a banking panic marking the climax of the banks' founding boom that led to the failure of many banks and encouraged Japanese policymakers to consolidate the banking system; not in crisisJST_old.
sources: Okazaki & Yokoyama (2002, 3-4); Sources: Tamaki (1995), Okazaki & Yokoyama (2002)

description: Payne & Rodgers (2014) identify economic shocks to mining in Japan as the trigger: a riot of workers and an adverse demand shock from the United States that reduced demand for natural resources. The economic problems of the mines harmed their regions and led to bank runs, the first in February 1907 at the Nagoya Bank, which was supported with 2.5 million yen from the government. In the following months bank runs and suspensions hit several banks in Tokyo and other areas, including the One Hundred Thirty-Eight Bank. During the first half of 1908, 42 banks were affected by runs and 23 banks suspended. In response the government sharply increased supporting loans to banks.
sources: Payne & Rodgers (2014); Sources: Inoue & Yabushita (1993), Payne & Rodgers (2014)

description: The prelude was the recession that started in 1919 after the end of the First World War, when the wartime export boom ended and current account deficits pressured the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates in late 1919. The rate increases weighed on the banking system and led to the Japanese 'Black Monday' when the securities and commodities markets collapsed, with loss of equity at large banks, contagion and bank runs. Between April and July 1920, 57 bank head offices and 102 branch offices were affected by runs and 21 banks were forced to close temporarily. The Bank of Japan supplied emergency loans amounting to 85.33 million yen to banks that needed reserves to sustain deposit withdrawals, and blamed risky lending practices and the issuance of non-transparent securities. Not identified by Bordo et al. (2001) or Reinhart & Rogoff (2009); identified by Baron et al. (2021). Section 5.4 treats the Baron et al. (2021) year 1922 as part of this episode because bank failures happened three years in a row.

The Great Kanto Earthquake of September 1923 damaged financial assets and real capital; the government was unable to solve the resulting problems, leading to a significant increase in non-performing loans that were at the centre of the 1927 crisis. Parliamentary debates and publications on the difficult financial situation of the Bank of Taiwan, Suzuki & Co and Tokyo Watanabe Bank caused a financial panic and sparked several bank runs. Tamaki (1995) lists four waves of bank bankruptcies: six banks including Imabari Shogyo and Fukaya Shogyo between the end of January and March; a second wave triggered by the closure of Watanabe Bank with 11 failures including Murai Bank and two Tokyo-based banks; a third wave from the beginning of April with four failures holding 8.5 million yen of paid-in capital; and a fourth beginning with the closure of the Bank of Taiwan, the giant Fifteen Bank (the 'Aristocratic Bank') and eleven further banks. The authorities increased loans to banks by 1,450 million yen. Section 5.4 rejects the Baron et al. (2021) year 1923 on the grounds that government intervention postponed the resulting systemic crisis until 1927.
sources: Tamaki (1995, pp. 151-152); Sources: Inoue & Yabushita (1993), Tamaki (1995)

description: Sharp declines in real estate and stock prices hurt Japanese banks and non-performing loans rose continuously in the following years. When growth slowed in 1997 the bank Sanyo Securities failed and started a chain reaction in the financial system: rising interbank market rates impeded bank funding and deteriorated liquidity, and within the same month Hokkaido Takushoku Bank (one of the eleven large city banks), Yamaichi Securities (the fourth largest securities firm) and Tokuyo City Bank (a regional bank) collapsed. The government undertook two rounds of capital injections: in the first round 23 banks including major banks applied for a total of 1.8 trillion yen (0.4 percent of GDP), and in the second round fifteen major banks received 7.5 trillion yen (1.5 percent of GDP). Section 5.4 rejects the Baron et al. (2021) year 1990 (bank share prices slumped sharply but there was no systemic crisis or panic; losses accumulated slowly up to 1997) and treats the Baron et al. (2021) year 2001 as part of the crisis that started in 1997.
sources: Nelson & Tanaka (2014, p. 41); Nelson & Tanaka (2014, p. 42); Sources: Harada (2001), Nelson & Tanaka (2014)

description: Grossman (2010) states that the war-related closure of the money market led to rapid growth of the banking sector in 1914-1920 and its increasingly close connection with industry; the downturn in 1921 led to bankruptcies of many small local banks and to intervention by the Netherlands Bank in favor of the mid-sized Bank-Associatie and Marx & Co. (1922) and the extremely large Rotterdamsche Bankvereeniging (1924). The crisis hit no less than fifty-nine banks, many of which failed; one conservative estimate puts the losses at 200 million florins in 1920-1922 alone. One of only two coded Dutch episodes after the removal of 1893, 1907 and 1939 in this version (Section 3.2).
sources: Grossman (2010, pp. 308-309); Jonker & van Zanden (1995, p. 80)

description: Part of the international crisis that started in the United States. While the ECB intervened as lender of last resort, the Dutch government reacted with deposit guarantees and launched a guarantee scheme for medium-term bank debt to address liquidity problems; it also committed to provide capital support for banks, which was used by ING Group, SNS Reaal and Aegon. ABN AMRO and Fortis Netherlands were nationalized. The measures and commitments to support financial institutions amounted to 52 percent of GDP (based on 2008).
sources: Sources: Kellermann (2009), Stolz & Wedow (2010, pp. 19-20)

description: From 1895 economic activity rose with the international upswing and the political decision to resume railway construction from Oslo, starting rising construction activity and speculation on land; real estate prices, the number of operating banks and lending rose sharply. In 1899 the failure of Chr Christophersen, a large non-financial firm, precipitated a crash in asset markets: dwelling prices fell 59 percent in Oslo (1899-1904) and 43 percent in Bergen (1898-1905). Two larger banks, Discontobanken and Industribanken, and the smaller Den Nordiske Aktiebank received considerable support from the Norges Bank, and Industribanken also from the central government; the smaller Kristiania Delkrederebank, Norsk Vexel- og Landmandsbank, Christiania Privatbank and Christiania Handelsbank were liquidated privately without intervention by the Norges Bank or the government. Bordo et al. (2001) do not identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1898.
sources: Sources: Gerdrup (2003, pp. 8-14), Grytten & Hunnes (2010, pp. 16-17)

description: The First World War ended Norway's participation in the international gold standard and the Scandinavian currency union; monetary expansion by the central bank and substantial export increases to the belligerents produced rising credit and growth, share prices rose significantly and many banks became more willing to finance risky stock market speculation. After the war, gold outflows and the European downturn led to a deflationary spiral with stock prices falling to their pre-war level and significant negative consequences for the banking system. Over the crisis years about 131 banks went bankrupt, were liquidated or merged, and losses reached new records. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1919.
sources: Sources: Gerdrup (2003, pp. 14-21), Grytten & Hunnes (2010, pp. 17-18)

description: Part of the world economic crisis that started in 1929 in the US. Norway had re-entered the gold standard in May 1928, which, as in many other European countries, was the main reason for the capital outflows that destabilized the banking system; its early exit from gold in September 1931 increased the Norges Bank's flexibility to react. Two large commercial banks were forced to apply for protection in the form of a three-month moratorium in November-December 1931 and were granted assurance of access to unlimited liquidity from the Norges Bank. Several smaller banks were either liquidated or stabilized with central bank and government assistance. From 1930 to 1934 the number of operating joint-stock commercial banks fell from 151 to 120 and the number of savings banks from 627 to 616.
sources: Sources: Bernanke & James (1991), Nordvik (1995), Grytten & Hunnes (2010, pp. 19-20)

description: In the 1980s the Norwegian government followed the international trend to liberalize credit and capital markets and the banking system to increase competition between intermediaries; overall expenditure and loans rose alongside increases in real estate and stock market prices of about 211 and 405 percent between 1980 and 1987 respectively. Tight fiscal and monetary policy in reaction to several foreign shocks then led to falling asset prices. In the following years several small and medium-sized banks failed, and the three biggest Norwegian banks, Kreditkassen, Fokus and Den norske Bank, lost large parts of their capital and were supported by the government. Losses of commercial banks rose from 2 percent to over 7 percent of total assets at the beginning of the 1990s; the gross recapitalization costs of the government amounted to 2.61 percent of GDP, and at the 1991 peak 16.4 percent of all loans were non-performing. Laeven & Valencia (2018) date the episode to 1991 and Baron et al. (2021) to 1987.
sources: Sources: Gerdrup (2003, pp. 21-27), Vale (2004), Grytten & Hunnes (2010, pp. 20-22), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: During the 1880s the Portuguese government steadily increased its stock of public debt; political problems in Brazil and increasing current account deficits reduced Portugal's credibility on international capital markets. When the Baring Crisis froze international capital markets and prompted foreign investors to reevaluate existing assets, Portugal lost access to new sources of funding and its banks lost the trust of the public. In 1890 the largest bank, Montepio Geral, witnessed the first problems, and the whole banking system was affected until 1891. To counter the fragility Portugal suspended the gold standard and the central bank intervened as lender of last resort. Bordo et al. (2001) do not identify a crisis.
sources: Sources: Branco et al. (2012)

description: After the First World War the Portuguese economy had similar problems to other European economies, namely the changed economic needs of society and an accelerating inflation rate. J. Reis (1995) argues the 1920 crisis was a banking panic whose causes were shocks from the real economy and a decline in the public's trust in banks. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1921.

The banking system struggled with the loss of public trust since the crisis of 1920. J. Reis (1995) argues that an adverse foreign demand shock combined with tight monetary policy created a recession, during which the already missing trust of the public manifested in a banking panic. The number of operating banks, which had increased since the 1920 crisis, reversed in 1923, and the number of operating joint-stock commercial banks declined from 28 to 21 by 1925.
sources: J. Reis (1995, pp. 480-482); Sources: J. Reis (1995)

description: Portugal was hit by the world economic crisis in 1930, but the crisis aggravated during 1931: the decline in international demand affected many Portuguese firms, which transmitted the shock to the financial system. Declining asset prices and write-offs caused the closure of five banks in 1932, of which the Banco do Minho and the Banco Português e Brasileiro were especially relevant. When the Banco Nacional Ultramarino, one of the most important Portuguese banks, was threatened by a possible failure, the government intervened to stabilize the banking system.
sources: Sources: J. Reis (1995)

description: Portugal's banks were already very large relative to the size of the economy, with a significant part of their liabilities consisting of foreign debt. When the crisis started in the US and Europe, Portugal experienced a 'sudden stop' of foreign capital and losses within its important banks. While the ECB intervened with broad liquidity support, the government increased the deposit guarantee from EUR 25,000 to EUR 100,000 and implemented a EUR 20 billion facility to guarantee the liabilities of Portuguese banks; the Banco Português de Negócios was nationalized. Support measures and commitments amounted to 12 percent of GDP (based on 2008). Baron et al. (2021) additionally flag 2011, which JST treats as linked to the 2008 crisis (Section 5.4).
sources: Pereira & Wemans (2015); Sources: Stolz & Wedow (2010, p. 20), Pereira & Wemans (2015), R. Reis (2013, pp. 172-179)

description: Liberalization of the financial and banking system in the 1860s and 1870s supported industrial development. During the boom of the 1870s Swedish banks shifted their focus to bonds and claims on railway companies, which had been categorized as safe; when the terms of trade deteriorated the railway companies incurred losses and became unable to service their debt. Consequences comprised bank runs and bank failures, including the bankruptcy of the Enskilda bank. The government intervened by creating the Railroad Mortgage Fund, where banks could pledge their unmarketable railroad bonds; the fund was worth SEK 23 million, corresponding to 8-9 percent of total public lending by commercial banks, but affected banks needed only a third of the rescue capital, the main part of which was taken by Stockholms Enskilda Bank. Not covered by Bordo et al. (2001).
sources: Sources: Knutsen & Sjögren (2009, pp. 16-20)

description: Part of the international financial panic that started in the United States. In the years before 1907 Swedish banks had borrowed on international capital markets to finance domestic credit; the worldwide panic denied them access to new funding, necessitating a reaction by the Swedish central bank. A total of 16 banks went bankrupt or were reconstituted, and the adverse effects of the crisis persisted until 1909.
sources: Hagberg & Jonung (2009, pp. 166-167)

description: A wartime boom with rising stock and asset prices and high inflation was followed by a political decision to return to the gold standard at the pre-war parity, which required restrictive monetary policy. Combined with a fall in foreign demand caused by post-war downturns in many European countries, this initiated a sharp recession and problems within the banking system: many banks incurred heavy losses and 14 commercial banks were liquidated. The government established the Credit Bank of 1922 to support the banks. Bordo et al. (2001) do not identify a crisis; Baron et al. (2021) date it to 1919.
sources: Nordvik (1995, pp. 453-455); Sources: Nordvik (1995), Hagberg & Jonung (2009, pp. 168-169), Grossman (2010, p. 310)

description: The Great Depression hit Sweden in late 1931: falling exports reduced aggregate demand, employment and industrial production, capital outflows drained the Riksbank's international reserves, and Sweden was forced to abandon gold and float the krona in September 1931 shortly after the pound, adopting a policy of price stabilization whose depreciation allowed it to isolate itself from the international turmoil (Hagberg & Jonung, 2009). Nonetheless serious problems in the banking system started when the death of the important industrialist Ivan Kreuger set off a series of bankruptcies that affected banks with strong business ties, such that the government intervened to secure banking stability. Baron et al. (2021) date the episode to 1932.
sources: Hagberg & Jonung (2009, p. 170); Sources: Hagberg & Jonung (2009, pp. 169-170)

description: Financial liberalization and a fixed exchange rate at the beginning of the 1980s were the starting points of strong credit growth and rising asset prices; Jonung et al. (2009a) emphasize that households took on high debt to finance a sharp increase in consumption and investment, especially in real estate. When interest rates in Europe started to rise in 1990, asset prices dropped. Bank credit losses accelerated during 1990 and 1991 to an annual rate of 3.5 percent of lending by the end of 1991 and 7.5 percent at the peak in the final quarter of 1992; accumulated losses over 1990-1993 came to nearly 17 percent of lending. First signs of solvency problems appeared in 1991 at Första Sparbanken and Nordbanken; despite a SEK 4.2 billion capital injection for Nordbanken and guarantees for Första Sparbanken in 1991, Nordbanken needed an additional capital injection by 1992, and Gota, the largest Swedish bank, was also supported by public equity. The total payment of the government to support Swedish banks was SEK 66.4 billion.
sources: Jonung et al. (2009a); Englund & Vihriälä (2009)

description: Part of the international financial crisis: several Swedish banks were affected by an increase in capital-market volatility and the general loss of confidence on interbank markets. The Swedish central bank intervened directly to stabilize banks by providing more liquidity in domestic and foreign currency and implementing facilities for banks to borrow kronor at longer maturities than usual. The government increased the limit for insured deposits from SEK 250,000 to SEK 500,000 and set up guarantees for the medium-term debt of banks and mortgage institutions of up to SEK 1.5 trillion. Two banks, Kaupthing Bank Sverige and Carnegie Investment Bank, were primarily affected and were sold to private investors with government assistance. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) do not identify a crisis; Laeven & Valencia (2018) and Baron et al. (2021) do.
sources: Molin (2009, pp. 138-140); Sources: Molin (2009), Laeven & Valencia (2018)

description: At the beginning of the 1870s many investors in the US and Europe invested heavily in US railroad bonds on the strength of stable returns over many years. When stock markets crashed in Europe in 1873, many European investors sold US securities, especially railroad bonds, depressing bond prices and making financing more expensive for the affected companies until they failed. Because many US banks held securities issued by those firms, a banking panic started: more than 40 brokerage houses (private banks) failed in September 1873 in New York, Philadelphia and Washington D.C., and one national bank and two trust companies failed in New York City. The loss of depositor confidence was confined to the savings banks, all of which suffered runs. Not covered by Bordo et al. (2001).
sources: Sources: Tallman & Wicker (2009, pp. 12-15), Richardson & Sablik (2015), Aliber & Kindleberger (2015, pp. 195-196)

description: Described as one of the severest financial crises of the national banking era, triggered by the failure of many railway companies and the collapse of the silver price, which affected many mines. These shocks led to a stock market crash in New York City and distrust against many banks; during 1893 vast amounts of deposits were withdrawn from financial centres and from banks in the interior of the United States, forcing many banks to sell assets in fire sales that depressed asset prices. Once New York and other financial centres refused to allow depositors to make large withdrawals in order to stop further fire sales, a banking panic affected many banks, especially those in the interior parts of the country. Over 500 national banks failed.
sources: Sources: Carlson (2005), Tallman & Wicker (2009, pp. 15-17), Richardson & Sablik (2015)

description: Seasonal transportation of crops and international gold flows caused money market rates to rise in autumn 1907. The Knickerbocker Trust Company, affected by the increasing cost of capital, suffered a loss of confidence due to its risky investments; when the main banks denied Knickerbocker access to clearing and the company failed, the loss of confidence gained momentum and resulted in a banking panic against banks and other trust companies, which operated outside the effective clearing regulation because of their low relevance for the payment system. The crisis eventually led to the establishment of the Federal Reserve.
sources: Tallman & Wicker (2009, p. 18); Sources: Tallman & Moen (1990), Tallman & Wicker (2009, pp. 17-20)

description: During the 1920s many banks engaged in speculation in several assets, especially stocks; from 1928 to 1929 the Federal Reserve aimed to curb speculation-driven asset prices through increases in the nominal interest rate, and the tight monetary policy ultimately led to the stock market crash of October 1929, marking the start of the Great Depression. Friedman & Schwartz (1963) argue that over the following years systematic bank panics and bank runs impaired the stability of the banking system and led to a significant decline in the money supply: the first important bank run occurred in October 1930 when several banks in the South and Midwest failed, the second in the spring of 1931, and the third in September 1931. The instability caused sharp declines in asset prices and reduced bank capital; over one-third of all banks failed during the Great Depression. Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) date the episode to 1929.
sources: Friedman & Schwartz (1963); Sources: Friedman & Schwartz (1963), Eichengreen & Temin (2000), Bernanke (2000)

description: The Savings and Loan (S&L) crisis. Sharp increases in the Federal Funds Rate in the late 1970s and early 1980s to stop rising inflation were an adverse shock for many S&Ls: rising interest rates reduced the net present value of their assets and the maturity mismatch between loans and deposits increased their costs. To support the S&Ls the government implemented a broad liberalization policy to improve their flexibility, but greater competitive pressure and higher risk-taking led to further declines in asset values and many S&Ls became insolvent; the sharp fall in oil prices in 1987 initiated declining real estate prices in several regions and brought the crisis to its peak (Grossman, 2010). During 1980-94 the FSLIC and RTC managed the resolution of nearly 1,300 S&Ls with over USD 620 billion in assets at a cost of more than USD 160 billion, while the FDIC managed the resolution of nearly 300 banks with assets of more than USD 900 billion at a cost of almost USD 200 billion. Laeven & Valencia (2018) date the episode to 1988; Section 5.4 rejects the Baron et al. (2021) year 1990 because at the beginning of 1989 there were no more systemic dangers arising from the banking system.
sources: Grossman (2010, pp. 270-271); Grossman (2010, p. 272)

description: Since the beginning of the 2000s real estate prices and credit growth gained momentum; banks engaged in securitization of mortgage loans (see Hellwig, 2008) and indirectly distributed growing risks within the whole US financial system, with growing dependence on short-term wholesale market financing for many intermediaries. When real estate prices started to fall in the summer of 2007, many banks had to take high write-offs and a financial panic erupted against many 'shadow banks', i.e. money market funds. The crisis reached its peak with the collapse of the investment bank Lehman Brothers and the near-collapse of the American International Group (AIG). Substantial government bail-outs and liquidity assistance by the Federal Reserve were necessary to stabilize the banking system. US measures and commitments to support financial institutions amounted to 26 percent of GDP (based on 2008). Not covered by Bordo et al. (2001).
sources: Hellwig (2008); Sources: Hellwig (2008), Stolz & Wedow (2010), Mian & Sufi (2014), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (2017)
